query: For Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 initially in a high-temperature BCC state, the factors governing its phase stability during cooling and subsequent thermal exposure are not understood well enough to account for the range of phases that may appear. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain this behavior and why? Define a controlled comparison and baseline, predicted observations relative to that baseline, the conditions under which the hypothesis should and should not apply, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification result.

generation.hypothesis: The phase instability and diverse phase evolution in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 is primarily driven by kinetically activated local lattice distortions from atomic size mismatch (especially induced by Al) that modulate defect densities (e.g., dislocations and grain boundaries) and trigger localized chemical partitioning. This in turn promotes the decomposition of the high-temperature BCC phase into distinct, metastable BCC variants and even secondary phases (e.g., HCP or FCC) during slow cooling or extended thermal exposure.
generation.material_initial_state: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 in a homogeneous high-temperature BCC phase.
generation.intervention: Apply controlled cooling protocols (varying cooling rates and annealing durations) to samples that begin in the high-temperature BCC state.
generation.conditions: The hypothesis should apply when the cooling rate is slow enough (or the thermal exposure is sufficiently long) to allow local atomic diffusion that relieves lattice strain via atomic shuffling (i.e., when the kinetics are not arrested) but may not apply under rapid quenching conditions where kinetic constraints freeze the high-temperature phase.
generation.structural_mediator: Local lattice distortions introduced by the atomic size mismatch (notably from Al) and the associated defect (dislocation, grain boundary) structures which serve as nucleation sites for local phase ordering and chemical segregation.
generation.mechanism: The large atomic size difference, particularly of Al relative to the transition metals, creates heterogeneous strain fields within the BCC lattice. These strains lower the energy barrier for local atomic shuffling and defect-assisted nucleation of secondary phases. During slow cooling or prolonged annealing, these localized distortions facilitate chemical partitioning leading to the observed metastable phase decompositions into, for example, two BCC variants and possibly, under certain conditions, secondary HCP or FCC phases.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under slow cooling or extended annealing, X-ray diffraction and microscopy will reveal increasing chemical heterogeneity, splitting of the BCC peak into components (indicative of bccL and bccH phases) and the emergence of secondary phase signatures (HCP or FCC) relative to the baseline high-temperature BCC state. In contrast, rapid cooling should largely preserve the single BCC phase due to arrested atomic mobility and suppressed chemical partitioning.
generation.baseline: Samples cooled rapidly from the high-temperature BCC state that show minimal phase decomposition and limited chemical segregation.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to be dominant in compositions where significant atomic size differences exist (e.g., due to the presence of Al) and when thermal energies enable local atomic diffusion. It may not apply or be masked in systems with minimal atomic size mismatch or in cases where processing parameters (e.g., extremely high cooling rates) preclude diffusion.
generation.uncertainty: While lattice distortions and defect-mediated diffusion are well-supported mechanisms in similar high-entropy alloys, the relative contributions of chemical driving forces versus kinetic barriers in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 remain uncertain and may vary with processing conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 samples from the high-temperature BCC state. Subject one set to rapid quenching and the other to slow cooling with intermediate annealing steps. Use controlled thermal exposure experiments in identical atmospheres to minimize extrinsic effects. Characterize phase composition using high-resolution X-ray diffraction, electron backscatter diffraction, and chemical mapping techniques.
measurements: XRD peak splitting and phase fraction analysis
Microstructural imaging (e.g., EBSD) for defect structure and phase distribution
EDS mapping for chemical segregation patterns
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If both the rapidly cooled and slowly cooled samples display statistically equivalent phase purity (i.e., a single homogeneous BCC phase) and show no measurable differences in defect structures or chemical segregation, then the hypothesized mechanism based on local lattice distortions and defect‐facilitated chemical partitioning is falsified.

Influence of SPD-Straining on the Annealing-Induced Changes in the Phase Composition and Microstructure In this study, the thermal stability of an HfNbTiZr MPEA processed by HPT for a broad range of shear strain between ~3 and ~340 was investigated. For all studied strains, an initial single-phase bcc structure decomposed into two separate bcc phases having lower and higher values of lattice constant, which is more dominant with increasing annealing temperature. In the sample with high strains, an additional hcp phase was also developed during annealing. The decomposition of the single bcc phase is consistent with former Calphad thermodynamic calculation performed on a similar MPEA composition (HfNbTaTiZr) []. The earlier study predicted a two-phase microstructure with a Zr/Hf/Ti-rich hcp main phase with the coexistence of a Nb/Ta-rich bcc structure below a temperature of about 970 K. Above 970 K, the hcp phase was gradually substituted with a Ti/Zr/Hf-rich bcc structure in the HfNbTaTiZr MPEA.
